usage: The weather is gradually getting colder
Pairs naturally with -아/어지다 verbs that show change over time
Common with progressive -고 있다 to stress an ongoing trend
My Korean is improving more and more
Everyday way to describe steady skill growth
점점 더 stacks for extra emphasis on the increase
examples: 요즘 물가가 점점 올라서 부담돼요.
Prices keep gradually rising these days, so it's a burden.
A very real complaint among residents about cost of living
운동을 시작하니까 몸이 점점 가벼워지는 것 같아요.
Since I started working out, my body feels gradually lighter.
점점 + change verb describing a positive trend
밤이 되니까 사람들이 점점 줄어들었어요.
As night fell, the crowd gradually thinned out.
Describes a slow decrease over time
nuance: 점점 describes a slow, steady change in one direction and almost always travels with a verb of change like 좋아지다, 추워지다, or 늘다. It is not used for sudden shifts. The variant 점점 더 adds emphasis, and 점차 is a more formal written cousin you'll see in news and notices.
mistakes: Using 점점 with a static verb like 점점 있어요 instead of a change verb such as 점점 많아져요
Confusing it with 갑자기 (suddenly); 점점 is always gradual, never abrupt

usage: Classic weather use; the change is abrupt and unexpected
Why are you acting like this all of a sudden?
Mild way to question an out-of-nowhere change in someone
Useful for describing a sudden physical symptom
Very common when you abruptly remember something
examples: 회사에서 갑자기 회식하자고 해서 약속을 취소했어요.
Work suddenly called a team dinner, so I canceled my plans.
갑자기 + unexpected work demand, a relatable scenario
멀쩡하던 노트북이 갑자기 꺼졌어요.
My laptop, which was totally fine, suddenly shut off.
Describes an abrupt malfunction
친구가 갑자기 연락이 안 돼서 걱정했어요.
My friend suddenly became unreachable, so I was worried.
Sudden change in an expected pattern
nuance: 갑자기 marks something abrupt and usually unplanned, often with a nuance of surprise or disruption. It is the direct opposite of 점점. Native speakers also use it conversationally to react to a sudden change in someone's mood or behavior, as in 갑자기 왜 이래요, which can sound slightly accusatory depending on tone.
mistakes: Spelling it 갑짜기; the correct form is 갑자기
Using it for slow changes where 점점 is needed, e.g. 갑자기 추워져요 sounds wrong for a gradual cooldown

usage: Expresses relief after a long wait or effort
Used after a long or tiring trip
Celebrating a result that took real effort
examples: 반년을 기다린 콘서트 표를 드디어 구했어요.
I finally got the concert ticket I'd waited half a year for.
드디어 + long-awaited positive outcome
드디어 비자가 나와서 마음이 놓여요.
My visa finally came through, so I feel relieved.
Very relevant to a foreign resident's life
야근이 끝나고 드디어 집에 가요.
Overtime is over and I'm finally going home.
Everyday relief after a hard day
nuance: 드디어 carries a strong sense of relief or satisfaction after a long anticipation, so it pairs with results the speaker actually wanted. It differs from 결국 (eventually/in the end), which can be neutral or even negative. Use 드디어 when there is a payoff worth celebrating, not just any final outcome.
mistakes: Using 드디어 for unwanted endings; 결국 fits a negative or neutral conclusion better
Treating it as 'finally' in the sense of listing steps (lastly); that meaning is 마지막으로, not 드디어

usage: Confirming that something lived up to its reputation
It's you, as I figured / you're the best
Warm praise meaning someone came through just like you knew
역시 can also mean 'also', similar to 또한
It's not working, just as I feared
examples: 이 집 김치찌개는 역시 최고예요.
This place's kimchi stew is the best, as expected.
역시 confirming a favorite spot stayed great
역시 출근 시간이라 지하철이 사람으로 꽉 찼어요.
Sure enough, it's rush hour, so the subway is packed.
Confirming an anticipated situation
고민하다가 역시 원래 계획대로 하기로 했어요.
After agonizing, I decided to go with the original plan after all.
역시 marking a return to what felt right all along
nuance: 역시 has two everyday senses: confirming that reality matched your expectation (sure enough), and a softer 'as I thought, X is great' that works as a compliment. As an interjection, 역시! on its own means 'I knew it / nailed it.' It can also mean 'also/too,' though that use is more formal and less common in casual speech.
mistakes: Overusing the 'also' meaning in casual talk where 도 or 또한 is more natural
Expecting it to mean 'again'; that is 다시 or 또, not 역시

english: rather, on the contrary, if anything
usage: Actually it worked out better that way
Reframes a seeming setback as a good thing
I apologized but instead they got angry
Marks a reaction opposite to what you'd expect
The expensive one is, if anything, worse
Contradicts the assumption that pricier means better
It's I who should be thanking you, rather
Politely flips a thank-you back onto yourself
examples: 지하철이 막힐 줄 알았는데 오히려 더 빨랐어요.
I thought the subway would be jammed, but it was actually faster.
오히려 introducing the opposite of an expectation
쉬려고 누웠는데 오히려 잠이 안 와요.
I lay down to rest, but instead I can't fall asleep.
Outcome contrary to the intended effect
혼날 줄 알았는데 사장님이 오히려 칭찬해 주셨어요.
I expected to get in trouble, but the boss praised me instead.
A surprising reversal in a workplace setting
nuance: 오히려 signals that the result runs counter to what you or the listener would naturally assume, often to a surprising or ironic degree. It frequently follows a clause with -는데 or -지만 that sets up the contrast. Think of it as 'contrary to expectation' rather than a simple 'instead,' which adds the flavor of a flipped assumption.
mistakes: Using it as a plain 'instead' for choosing between options; 대신에 fits that better
Forgetting the setup clause, so the contrast 오히려 needs has nothing to push against

english: when it actually comes to it, in reality, faced with it
usage: When I actually tried it, it was easy
Reality turning out different from what you imagined
Now that it's actually time to go, I can't be bothered
The moment of doing it changes how you feel
When it actually comes down to it, you end up doing it all
A common reassurance about rising to the occasion
I wanted to buy it, but seeing it in person, it's not great
Anticipation not matching the real thing
examples: 이직하고 싶었는데 막상 그만두려니까 망설여져요.
I wanted to switch jobs, but now that I'm actually about to quit, I hesitate.
막상 contrasting a wish with the reality of acting on it
발표가 걱정됐는데 막상 시작하니까 괜찮았어요.
I was worried about the presentation, but once I actually started, it was fine.
막상 + 시작하니까 showing the gap between dread and reality
월급날만 기다렸는데 막상 받으니까 카드값으로 다 나갔어요.
I only waited for payday, but when I actually got paid, it all went to the credit card bill.
막상 marking a letdown when the awaited moment arrives
nuance: 막상 sets up a contrast between what you expected, planned, or imagined and what actually happens once you face the real situation. It very often pairs with -(으)니까 or -(으)려니까 to mark that moment of confronting reality. The flavor is 'in theory I thought X, but actually Y,' so it shines when the real experience defies your prior assumption.
mistakes: Using it for a plain 'actually/really' fact; that is 사실 or 정말, while 막상 specifically means 'when faced with the real moment'
Dropping the setup, so there is no expectation for 막상 to contradict; it needs a prior assumption or plan to push against

english: anyway, in any case, either way
usage: Accepting a fixed reality as the basis for what follows
It's something I have to do either way
Frames a task as unavoidable regardless of choice
States a settled outcome that won't change
It's the same in any case
Dismisses a distinction as ultimately irrelevant
examples: 어차피 집에 가는 길이니까 같이 가요.
I'm headed home anyway, so let's go together.
어차피 presenting a fact that makes the suggestion easy
어차피 환불도 안 되는데 그냥 써야죠.
It's non-refundable anyway, so I'll just use it.
Resignation to an unchangeable condition
고민해도 어차피 결과는 안 바뀌어요.
No matter how much I worry, the result won't change either way.
어차피 stressing that effort won't alter the outcome
nuance: 어차피 sets up a premise that is already decided or unavoidable, so the speaker reasons from it: since X is fixed anyway, Y. It often carries a tone of resignation or pragmatic acceptance. It pairs naturally with -니까 or -는데 to connect the fixed fact to the conclusion the speaker draws from it.
mistakes: Using it for a simple 'anyway' that just changes topics; that conversational filler is 아무튼 or 어쨌든
Placing it where the outcome is still open; 어차피 assumes the result is already settled

english: (not) particularly, go out of one's way to, deliberately
usage: You don't have to go out of your way to do it
Most common use, telling someone not to bother
Questions why someone is making unnecessary effort
If I had to pick / strictly speaking
Set phrase for reluctantly choosing when pressed
I went all the way out there (when I didn't need to)
Highlights effort that wasn't really necessary
examples: 굳이 비싼 데 가지 말고 그냥 편의점에서 사 먹어요.
Let's not bother going somewhere expensive; let's just grab something at the convenience store.
굳이 + negative, discouraging needless effort
바쁘면 굳이 안 와도 되니까 부담 갖지 마세요.
If you're busy, you don't have to come, so don't feel pressured.
Polite, considerate use telling someone not to overextend
굳이 따지자면 저는 매운 음식이 더 좋아요.
If I had to choose, I prefer spicy food.
The fixed phrase 굳이 따지자면 for a forced preference
nuance: 굳이 conveys 'going out of one's way' for something not strictly necessary, and it shines in negative or rhetorical sentences like 굳이 안 해도 돼 (no need to bother). Used positively, it implies someone insisted on doing something despite it being unneeded. Korean speakers in their 20s-30s also use it as a one-word reaction, 굳이?, meaning 'is that really necessary?'
mistakes: Translating it as plain 'definitely'; that is 꼭 or 반드시, whereas 굳이 implies unnecessary effort
Forgetting that its most natural home is negative sentences, e.g. 굳이 안 사도 돼요

english: by nature, originally so much, inherently
usage: Gives an underlying reason rooted in a stable trait
It's an inherently very famous place
I just can't handle spicy food at all
Because there are just so many people (as usual)
Explains a situation by an inherent, baseline condition
examples: 그 식당은 워낙 줄이 길어서 예약하는 게 나아요.
That restaurant inherently has such long lines that it's better to reserve.
워낙 giving the baseline reason for advice
제 룸메이트는 워낙 조용해서 집에 있는지도 몰라요.
My roommate is so quiet by nature that I can't even tell if they're home.
워낙 describing an inherent personality trait
요즘 워낙 물가가 비싸서 외식을 줄였어요.
Prices are just so high these days that I've cut back on eating out.
워낙 + 아서/어서 explaining a consequence
nuance: 워낙 emphasizes that something is the way it is by its fundamental nature or to an inherently high degree, often setting up a reason with -아서/어서. It is close to 'so much by nature' and feels more grounded than 너무, because it points to a stable, baseline truth rather than a momentary feeling. It frequently explains why a predictable outcome follows.
mistakes: Swapping it for 너무 to mean a temporary 'too much'; 워낙 implies an inherent, ongoing degree
Using it without a follow-up reason or result; 워낙 usually leads into an explanation, not a standalone statement

usage: Why do you keep doing that?
Expresses mild irritation at repeated behavior
They keep contacting me over and over
If you keep seeing it, it grows on you
A common saying about repeated exposure
examples: 인터넷이 자꾸 끊겨서 통신사에 전화했어요.
The internet keeps cutting out, so I called the provider.
자꾸 + recurring problem prompting action
다이어트 중인데 자꾸 야식이 생각나요.
I'm on a diet, but I keep thinking about late-night snacks.
자꾸 for a repeated urge you can't shake
옆집에서 자꾸 시끄럽게 해서 스트레스를 받아요.
The neighbors keep being noisy, so it stresses me out.
Repeated nuisance from others
nuance: 자꾸 means something happens again and again, and it usually carries a slightly negative or exasperated nuance, as if the repetition is bothersome or beyond control. It differs from 자주 (often), which is a neutral frequency word; 자꾸 emphasizes persistence and is frequently used to gently complain. It pairs well with verbs of habit or recurring trouble.
mistakes: Treating it as a neutral 'often'; for plain frequency use 자주, since 자꾸 implies pesky repetition
Using it for scheduled regular events like 자꾸 운동해요; 규칙적으로 or 자주 fits planned routines better

english: for a long while, quite a while
usage: I waited for a good while
I haven't seen (them) for quite a while
한참 동안 stresses the long stretch of time
It's still a long way off
Used for distance or 'far from done'
Marks a sizable gap before the next event
examples: 버스가 안 와서 정류장에서 한참 기다렸어요.
The bus didn't come, so I waited at the stop for a good while.
한참 describing a long, somewhat tedious wait
오랜만에 만난 친구랑 한참 수다를 떨었어요.
I chatted for ages with a friend I hadn't seen in a long time.
한참 for an extended enjoyable activity
이거 다 하려면 아직 한참 멀었어요.
There's still a long way to go before this is all done.
한참 멀었다 meaning far from finished
nuance: 한참 refers to a fairly long, indefinite stretch of time and feels more vivid and conversational than a precise 오래. It is the natural choice for describing waiting, talking, or walking that drags on. In the phrase 한참 멀었다 it shifts to mean 'far away' or 'nowhere near done,' covering both distance and progress.
mistakes: Using it as an exact duration; 한참 is deliberately vague, unlike 한 시간 (one hour)
Confusing 한참 (a long while) with 한창 (in full swing/at the peak); they look similar but mean different things

usage: Adds a 'more than expected' nuance to the adjective
Modifies a degree higher than anticipated
There are quite a lot of people
Remarking that a number is notably high
examples: 이 동네는 생각보다 꽤 조용하고 살기 좋아요.
This neighborhood is quite a bit quieter and nicer to live in than I expected.
꽤 + 생각보다 stressing it exceeded expectations
면접이 꽤 어려웠지만 그래도 잘 봤어요.
The interview was fairly tough, but I still did well.
꽤 setting a moderately high degree
새로 생긴 카페가 꽤 인기가 많더라고요.
The newly opened cafe turned out to be quite popular.
꽤 noting a higher-than-assumed degree
nuance: 꽤 means 'quite' or 'fairly' and often implies the degree is higher than the speaker expected, giving a faint note of surprise. It is stronger than 좀 (a little) but softer than 너무 or 정말, making it a handy mid-level intensifier. The near-synonym 꽤나 adds emphasis, and 꽤 sits comfortably in casual everyday speech.
mistakes: Treating it as 'too much'; that is 너무, while 꽤 stays at a moderate-to-notable level
Using it with negatives oddly, e.g. 꽤 안 좋아요 sounds off; prefer 별로 좋지 않아요 for 'not that good'
